text: map, filter, and reduce replace most hand-written for loops over arrays in modern code. Today covers exactly what each one does on its own, and how naturally all three chain together into a single readable expression.

map runs a function on every single element and returns a brand new array of the results, the same length as the original array every time — the original array itself is never changed in the process. Use it whenever you want the same list back, but with each item transformed, which is exactly what formatting a list of raw balances for display actually looks like in practice.

filter runs a test function on every element and returns a new array containing only the elements where that test returned true. The result can end up shorter than the original array, or even come back completely empty, if nothing in the array happens to pass the test.

reduce is the one that trips people up first, every time. It walks the entire array, carrying an accumulator forward from one element to the next, and returns one single final value at the end. The second argument you pass to reduce is the accumulator's starting point, and on each step the function returns the new accumulator value to carry into the next step.

These three chain together naturally: filter down to what actually matters, map to pull out just the one field you need, then reduce down to a single total. Filter, then map, then reduce over a list of transactions is close to exactly what real blockchain code does constantly when summarizing on-chain activity.

You're ready for lesson thirteen when you can chain filter, map, and reduce together on one array to answer a single question about its contents, in one expression. map transforms, filter selects, reduce collapses to one value, and all three chain together cleanly. Next up: spread and rest operators — two more pieces of syntax you'll see on almost every page of real code.
